conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you today. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’ve been having really bad nausea and vomiting all morning. It’s like my usual gastroparesis flare, but worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any abdominal pain, fever, or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no pain or fever. But I did throw up a little blood when I got here. That scared me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’ll keep an eye on that. You also mentioned chills—any other new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just the chills since I’ve been here. Otherwise, same as usual—just can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We gave you Zofran and Ativan in the ER for nausea. After the Ativan, your breathing slowed and oxygen dropped, so we moved you to ICU for monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wait—was that because of the Ativan? I’ve taken it before without problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was likely the 1 mg IV dose. You usually take 0.25 mg by mouth, right? Higher IV doses can affect breathing, especially if you're already unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So I should avoid higher doses then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll make a note in your chart. You’re breathing fine now, which is great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back. Blood sugar was high—302 this morning. We’re watching for signs of DKA, but you’re not in it. We adjusted your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sugars have been running high lately. Did we figure out why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely due to vomiting—you can’t keep food or meds down, so insulin balance gets thrown off. We’re giving you IV fluids and adjusting your coverage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about the blood I vomited?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s from a small tear in the esophagus—called a Mallory-Weiss tear—caused by forceful vomiting. Your hemoglobin is stable, so no active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’ve stopped your aspirin temporarily and started a stronger stomach protector—Protonix twice daily for six weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood pressure spiked last night—up to 215/140. That’s called hypertensive urgency. We gave IV meds to bring it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was that because of the vomiting or stress?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely both, and you couldn’t take your lisinopril by mouth. We restarted it today now that you’re tolerating liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Are my sugars better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ve come down with adjusted insulin. We’ll keep monitoring and get you back to your home regimen before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added IV erythromycin. It helps with stomach emptying and might be useful for your gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve never taken that before. Is it safe with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve checked. It’s a short course. We’ll stop it when you leave, but you should discuss continuing it with your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. You’ve kept down clear liquids and your nausea is less. We’re going to try small amounts of soft food today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’m hungry, but I’m nervous about vomiting again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. We’ll go slow—small bites, frequent checks. If you keep it down, we’ll advance further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great job—you tolerated applesauce and crackers. We’re upgrading to a soft diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my gastric pacer? It hasn’t been helping as much lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. Dr. ___ is back next week. We’ll schedule a pacer check to see if it needs adjustment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is still a bit high, but more stable. We used hydralazine for peaks, but now it’s mostly controlled with your usual meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I worry about my heart? My dad died of heart disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your EKG—it shows sinus tachycardia and some changes from high BP, but no signs of heart attack. Controlling your pressure helps reduce long-term risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. That helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray and abdominal film were normal. The pacer is in place, and no signs of blockage or free air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. Any other tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a MRSA screen—negative, so no infection concern. Main issues remain gastroparesis, blood pressure, and blood sugar control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. You’re on a regular diet, no vomiting, and labs are stable. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What meds will I go home on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before: Reglan, lisinopril, clonidine, Protonix, and insulin. We’re adding a low-dose lorazepam for nausea—only half a 0.5 mg pill if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no more Ativan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can take the lorazepam—it’s the same drug family—but only half your usual dose. Avoid anything higher due to your breathing reaction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the erythromycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping it here, but bring it up with your GI doctor. It seemed to help, so they might want to continue it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. You’re stable, eating well, and symptoms are controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Any warning signs I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—call if nausea or vomiting returns, or if you see blood in vomit or stool. Also watch for high blood sugar, severe headache, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your GI doctor soon to discuss the pacer and erythromycin. Also follow up with your endocrinologist about insulin management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to come back if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure all my doctors know about the Ativan reaction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. That’s very important for your safety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll advance my diet slowly at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Small meals, low fat, low fiber. Avoid heavy or greasy foods that can trigger symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. We’re discharging you home in stable condition. Take it easy and follow up soon.
